extracted.intended_audience: newsroom editors, journalists, media organizations, and readers interested in journalism ethics and AI
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for using AI to produce news content in a newsroom setting, focusing on disclosure, editorial standards, plagiarism prevention, and appropriate task assignment. Emphasizes what news organizations must do (and not do) when deploying AI-generated articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent disclosure of AI use
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly disclose when an article was produced by an AI rather than hiding or obscuring that fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post criticizes CNET for not properly disclosing AI authorship; vague language like “generated using automation technology” or attributing pieces to generic staff is insufficient. Proper disclosure would make it clear to readers that the content was AI-generated and not written by human reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate bylines and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Bylines and author attribution must honestly reflect authorship (human or AI) and not falsely attribute AI work to staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNET attributed AI-written pieces to “CNET Money Staff,” which hid the true source. The byline page itself was unclear; accurate bylines should not falsely suggest human staff authorship when AI produced the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear provenance and training transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose which AI system was used and how it was trained or sourced, especially if training data may include third-party content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes uncertainty about which AI CNET used and how it was trained, raising concerns that the AI may have been trained on scraped content it later paraphrased. Newsrooms should be transparent about model provenance and training data where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper wording of automation disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise, unambiguous language when describing automation—distinguish between 'automation technology' and 'AI' and state explicitly what was done by machine vs human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that phrasing matters: saying an article was “generated using automation technology” may mislead readers compared with explicitly stating it was written by an AI. Disclosures should avoid euphemisms and be explicit about the machine’s role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human editorial oversight and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated content must be subjected to thorough human editing, fact-checking, and polishing before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece emphasizes that AI requires humans to edit, fact-check, and add expertise; CNET’s claim that humans were editing and fact-checking failed given the number of factual errors found. Editors should be able to review notes, check sources, and apply subject-matter expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher level of verification for AI outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Because AI is a 'black box', outputs should receive equal or greater scrutiny than human-written content, not less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that AI needs even more rigorous checking than human reporters because reasoning and source use are opaque. A prompt-in/text-out process requires extra layers of validation to prevent misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AI only for appropriate tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign AI to constrained, suitable tasks (e.g., fill-in-the-blank or templated reporting) rather than complex reporting requiring judgment and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites the Washington Post’s Heliograf as an example of limited, appropriate AI use. It warns against using AI where the goal is to replace substantive human judgment or reduce human involvement in complex stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent and detect plagiarism / ensure originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure AI output is original and does not simply rewrite or paraphrase existing sources in a way that constitutes plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNET’s AI produced short passages that closely mirrored source material, amounting to plagiarism even if brief. The author notes that poor paraphrasing is common and must be guarded against; short rewritten passages can be plagiarism even if not necessarily copyright infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use and limits of plagiarism-detection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must correctly use plagiarism-detection tools and not rely solely on them; tools can miss problems and require human follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNET’s editor-in-chief blamed failures on plagiarism checkers either not being used or missing issues. The post warns that tools can fail and editors must apply manual scrutiny when checking AI content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish plagiarism from copyright infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that short rewritten passages can be plagiarism (ethically unacceptable) even if they may not rise to legal copyright infringement on their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observes that the problematic passages were short rewrites that likely would not sustain a copyright claim alone, but are clearly plagiarism. Newsrooms should address ethical plagiarism issues separate from legal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional responsibility for disclosure decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The newsroom leadership is responsible for decisions about disclosure and must bear institutional accountability for non-disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states that the AI did not decide to hide its use—CNET did—and that reflects worse on the institution. Policies and oversight must ensure truthful disclosure practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remediation: auditing, corrections, and pausing deployments
rubrics_metrics.description: When problems are found, conduct audits, add corrections, and consider pausing AI deployments until issues are resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNET performed an audit and added corrections; the author notes that pausing the program is appropriate but worries about plans to restart. Effective remediation includes thorough audits and public corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prioritize cost-cutting over quality and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid deploying AI primarily to reduce headcount or costs at the expense of journalistic standards and institutional reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post argues that if the goal is fewer humans on pieces, AI is not the right route; cutting human involvement led to worse quality and reputational harm for CNET.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using low-quality article-spinning tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on scraping-and-spinning or automated paraphrasing techniques that produce low-quality, derivative content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author compares CNET’s AI output to old article spinners and automated paraphrasing tools, noting the output looked like low-quality rewriting rather than genuinely new text; newsrooms should avoid such approaches.
